**[Section 4: HIPAA Business Associate Agreement Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Failure to execute a compliant BAA with a vendor that processes PHI exposes Pinnacle to enforcement action by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (\"**OCR**\"), including civil monetary penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year (as adjusted for inflation). Equally important, the absence of a BAA means that any disclosure of PHI to the vendor may itself constitute a HIPAA violation.

ALL vendors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on Pinnacle\'s behalf must execute a BAA. There are no exceptions to this requirement. This Section sets forth the must-have, nice-to-have, and fallback positions for BAA terms, as well as non-negotiable red lines.
**[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.
The BAA must specify, at a minimum, the following terms:

> **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. The BAA should enumerate the specific permitted purposes and should include a catch-all restriction providing that any use or disclosure not expressly authorized is prohibited.

> **(b) Minimum Necessary Standard.** The BAA must require vendor compliance with the \"minimum necessary\" standard set forth in 45 CFR § 164.502(b). Vendor must limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of each use, disclosure, or request. Vendor must implement policies and procedures to identify the workforce members who need access to PHI and to limit each such workforce member\'s access to the minimum PHI necessary for that person\'s role.

> **(c) Workforce Training.** Vendor must train all workforce members who have access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements. Training must be provided upon hiring and at least annually thereafter. Vendor must maintain documentation of training completion and make such documentation available to Pinnacle upon reasonable request.
> **(d) HIPAA Security Rule Safeguards.** Vendor must implement and maintain safeguards consistent with the three categories of the HIPAA Security Rule:
> \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.

> **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). This flow-down obligation must be contractually documented between vendor and each such subcontractor before PHI is made available to the subcontractor.
> **(f) Breach Notification.** The BAA must include breach notification obligations consistent with the HITECH Act requirements, as described in detail in Section 5 of this playbook.

> **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). This includes the BAA itself, policies and procedures relating to the protection of PHI, workforce training records, incident response records, and risk assessment documentation.

> **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.

**Nice-to-have:** The BAA should be integrated directly into the DPA body rather than attached as a separate exhibit. Integration reduces the risk of gaps in coverage that can arise when the DPA and BAA are separate documents with potentially inconsistent terms, different effective dates, or different amendment procedures. An integrated BAA also simplifies contract management and ensures that the BAA\'s security and audit provisions are consistent with the corresponding DPA provisions.

**Fallback:** A standalone BAA exhibit is acceptable if the following conditions are met: (i) the BAA exhibit is expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference; (ii) the BAA cross-references the DPA\'s security, audit, and breach notification provisions to ensure consistency; (iii) the BAA is executed simultaneously with the DPA and by the same authorized signatories; and (iv) the BAA includes a provision stating that, in the event of a conflict between the BAA and the DPA, the more protective provision governs with respect to the handling of PHI.
**[4.2 BAA Negotiation Red Lines]{.underline}**

Pinnacle will **NOT** execute a DPA without a conforming BAA where the vendor processes PHI. This is a **non-negotiable requirement** driven by federal law. No business justification, no vendor relationship importance, and no time pressure overrides this requirement.

If a vendor refuses to execute a BAA, or if a vendor\'s proposed BAA is materially deficient and the vendor refuses to negotiate acceptable terms, the negotiator must **escalate immediately** to Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel, and to Rachel Osterfeld at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP. Under no circumstances should a negotiator proceed with DPA execution in the absence of a conforming BAA.

For context, Pinnacle currently has approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts** whose PHI may be processed by vendors in the course of providing services to Pinnacle. The regulatory and reputational exposure associated with unauthorized disclosure of this PHI is substantial. OCR enforcement actions in recent years have resulted in settlements and penalties ranging from \$100,000 to over \$16 million for HIPAA violations involving inadequate BAA protections.

Negotiators should also be aware that some vendors may propose a \"HIPAA addendum\" or \"healthcare data supplement\" that purports to address HIPAA requirements but does not contain all of the mandatory BAA provisions listed in Section 4.1 above. Such documents must be carefully reviewed against the checklist in Section 4.1, and any missing provisions must be added before execution.

Breach notification provisions are among the most operationally significant terms in any DPA. The speed and completeness of vendor breach notification directly affects Pinnacle\'s ability to assess the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and meet its own notification obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s breach notification requirements, which are in certain respects **more restrictive** than the standalone requirements of any single applicable regulation.

Pinnacle\'s internal data breach response standard, as adopted by the Board of Directors in October 2023, requires that the Company\'s Incident Response Team be activated within **four (4) hours** of receiving vendor notification of a breach or suspected breach. This internal standard drives the 24-hour vendor notification requirement described below; a vendor notification timeline of 48 hours or longer is insufficient to support Pinnacle\'s internal response protocols and downstream regulatory obligations.

**Must-have:** Vendor must notify Pinnacle of any actual or reasonably suspected breach of Personal Data, PHI, or California Personal Information within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. For purposes of this requirement, \"**discovery**\" means the first day on which the breach is known to the vendor, or the first day on which the breach, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to the vendor. This definition is consistent with the HITECH Act\'s definition of discovery at 42 U.S.C. § 17382.

The 24-hour notification obligation applies regardless of whether the breach is confirmed or still under investigation. Pinnacle recognizes that a vendor\'s initial notification may be preliminary and that additional information will become available as the investigation proceeds. However, the failure to provide timely preliminary notification --- even where the full scope of the breach is not yet known --- deprives Pinnacle of the ability to initiate its own assessment and response activities.

> • The **72-hour timeline** referenced in GDPR Article 33(1) is the *controller\'s* obligation to notify the *supervisory authority*, not the processor\'s obligation to notify the controller. GDPR Article 33(2) requires processors to notify controllers \"without undue delay after becoming aware\" of a breach, which the European Data Protection Board has interpreted as requiring notification significantly faster than 72 hours.

> • A **48-hour** processor-to-controller timeline is insufficient because it compresses Pinnacle\'s time to assess the breach, engage legal counsel, activate its incident response plan, and prepare its own regulatory notifications. Under HIPAA, Pinnacle must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, and discovery is deemed to occur when the Business Associate notifies the Covered Entity. Under CCPA/CPRA, California\'s data breach notification statute (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.82) requires notification \"in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.\" Every hour of delay in vendor notification reduces Pinnacle\'s available response window.

> • Pinnacle\'s **24-hour standard** is consistent with market practice for healthcare data processing engagements and is required by multiple state breach notification statutes that apply to Pinnacle.
**[5.2 HIPAA-Specific Breach Notification Obligations]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must include the full HIPAA/HITECH breach notification cascade, reflecting the following obligations:

> **(a)** Vendor (as Business Associate) notifies Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery of a breach of Unsecured PHI. This notification triggers Pinnacle\'s own assessment and notification obligations.

> **(b)** Pinnacle notifies affected individuals within **sixty (60) days** of discovery of the breach, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.404. The notification must be in writing, sent by first-class mail to the individual\'s last known address (or by email if the individual has agreed to electronic notice), and must include the elements specified in 45 CFR § 164.404(c).
> • For breaches affecting **500 or more individuals**: notification to the HHS Secretary within **sixty (60) days** of discovery, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.408.

> • For breaches affecting **fewer than 500 individuals**: notification to the HHS Secretary no later than **sixty (60) days after the end of the calendar year** in which the breach was discovered, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.408(c).

> **(d)** For breaches affecting **500 or more residents** of a state or jurisdiction, Pinnacle must notify **prominent media outlets** serving that state or jurisdiction within **sixty (60) days** of discovery, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.406.

The DPA/BAA must clearly allocate responsibility for each step of this notification cascade. While vendor (as Business Associate) is responsible for the initial notification to Pinnacle, Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) is responsible for notifications to individuals, HHS, and the media. However, vendor must provide Pinnacle with all information reasonably necessary to enable Pinnacle to fulfill its notification obligations.
**Must-have:** Vendor\'s breach notification to Pinnacle must include, at a minimum, the following information:
> \(i\) The nature of the breach, including a description of what happened and the circumstances of the unauthorized access, use, or disclosure;
> \(ii\) The types of PHI involved in the breach (e.g., names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, diagnoses, treatment information, health plan identification numbers);
> \(iii\) The identification of each individual whose PHI was, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of the breach;
> \(iv\) A description of steps that affected individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach;
> \(v\) A description of what vendor is doing to investigate the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and prevent future breaches; and

> **Preferred position:** Vendor shall pay Pinnacle liquidated damages of **\$5,000 per day** for each day that vendor\'s breach notification is late (i.e., each day beyond the 24-hour notification deadline), with **no cap** on the total amount of liquidated damages. The parties acknowledge that the harm to Pinnacle from late notification is difficult to quantify and that this amount represents a reasonable estimate of such harm.
Regardless of the applicable regulatory regime, all breach notifications from vendor to Pinnacle must include the following minimum content:
> \(a\) The **nature and scope** of the breach, including a description of the incident and the systems, databases, or facilities affected;
> \(b\) The **categories and approximate number of data subjects or individuals** affected by the breach;

> \(d\) The **likely consequences** of the breach for affected data subjects or individuals, including an assessment of the risk of identity theft, financial harm, reputational harm, or harm to physical safety;
> \(e\) The **measures taken or proposed** by vendor to address the breach, including containment measures, remediation steps, and measures to prevent recurrence;

Liability provisions are among the most heavily negotiated terms in any DPA. The allocation of financial risk between Pinnacle and its vendors must reflect the magnitude of the data at stake, the severity of potential regulatory penalties, and the operational and reputational harm that a data breach or compliance failure could cause. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required liability framework, including liability caps, carve-outs, and indemnification obligations.

Pinnacle\'s position on liability is informed by the following considerations: (i) a breach of PHI affecting Pinnacle\'s approximately 2.1 million US patients could result in HIPAA penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year, plus class action litigation exposure; (ii) a CCPA/CPRA violation could result in statutory damages of \$100 to \$750 per consumer per incident, which at 890,000 California residents represents potential exposure of \$89 million to \$667.5 million; and (iii) GDPR penalties can reach up to €20 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Against this backdrop, vendor liability caps that are a fraction of annual fees are commercially unreasonable and legally inadequate.
**Must-have:** Vendor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under the DPA must be no less than **two times (2x) the total annual fees** attributable to the affected data processing activity.
> \(a\) **Willful misconduct** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
> \(b\) **Gross negligence** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
> \(d\) **Regulatory fines or penalties** imposed on Pinnacle as a direct result of vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws, including HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR.

**Must-have:** Consequential, indirect, and special damages may **NOT** be excluded for data breaches involving willful misconduct by vendor. A blanket consequential damages exclusion that applies to all claims, including data protection claims, is unacceptable. While mutual exclusions of consequential damages are common in general commercial agreements, they are inappropriate in the data protection context where the most significant harms to Pinnacle --- including regulatory penalties, class action settlements, breach notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, and reputational damage --- may be characterized as consequential or indirect damages under applicable law. A blanket exclusion could effectively eliminate vendor accountability for the very harms the DPA is intended to address.

**Nice-to-have:** A separate, higher \"**super-cap**\" for data protection claims (e.g., **3x annual fees**) that sits above the general MSA liability cap. This approach allows the parties to maintain a standard liability cap for general commercial claims under the MSA while providing enhanced protection for data protection claims under the DPA. For example, where annual fees are \$4.2 million, the general MSA cap might be \$4.2 million (1x) while the DPA super-cap would be \$12.6 million (3x).

**Fallback:** If vendor insists on a single aggregate cap covering both general commercial claims and data protection claims, the minimum acceptable cap is **2x total annual fees** (\$8,400,000 for a \$4.2 million annual engagement). Pinnacle will not accept a DPA liability cap below this threshold. Any vendor proposal below 2x annual fees must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park for review and decision.

**Note for negotiators:** Vendor templates frequently propose caps that are a small fraction of annual fees. It is not uncommon for a vendor with annual fees of several million dollars to propose a DPA liability cap of €500,000 or \$1,000,000. Such caps are commercially unreasonable given the regulatory exposure described above and the volume of data at stake. Negotiators should be prepared to provide the regulatory exposure calculations above as support for Pinnacle\'s 2x annual fees position.

> \(a\) **Third-party claims** (including claims by data subjects, consumers, patients, and healthcare providers) arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or any applicable data protection law;

> \(c\) **Costs of breach response**, including but not limited to: costs of breach notification to affected individuals and regulatory authorities; costs of credit monitoring and identity theft protection services provided to affected individuals; costs of forensic investigation; costs of public relations and crisis communications; and costs of regulatory reporting and compliance remediation, in each case to the extent arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or applicable data protection law.

Indemnification obligations should be subject to the same uncapped/capped structure as direct liability set forth in Section 6.1 above. Specifically, indemnification for claims arising from willful misconduct, gross negligence, intentional breaches of confidentiality, and regulatory fines resulting from vendor non-compliance must be uncapped. Indemnification for all other claims may be subject to the aggregate liability cap (2x annual fees), but must not be subject to any lower cap or sublimit.
**[Section 7: CCPA / CPRA Service Provider Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section sets forth the mandatory contractual provisions that must appear in all DPAs where the vendor processes personal information of California residents on Pinnacle\'s behalf. These provisions are required to establish the vendor\'s status as a \"Service Provider\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which is essential to Pinnacle\'s compliance with the statute.
**Must-have:** The DPA must include the following CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag):

> **(b) Purpose Limitation.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle for any purpose other than performing the services specified in the DPA and the applicable MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement. Vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information for vendor\'s own business purposes, including but not limited to marketing, product development, analytics, or profiling, unless such use is expressly authorized by Pinnacle in writing and is consistent with a permissible business purpose under the CCPA/CPRA.

> **(d) Prohibition on Combining.** Vendor is prohibited from combining personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information that vendor receives from or on behalf of any other person or entity, or that vendor collects from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA (e.g., to detect data security incidents or protect against fraud).

> **(e) Service Provider Certification.** Vendor must include a certification, executed by an authorized representative of vendor, stating that vendor understands the restrictions set forth in subparagraphs (a) through (d) above and will comply with them. This certification is a statutory requirement under the CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and must appear in the DPA itself or in a CCPA/CPRA Addendum appended to the DPA.

> **(f) Right to Monitor Compliance.** Vendor must grant Pinnacle the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that vendor uses personal information in a manner consistent with Pinnacle\'s obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. This includes the right to conduct ongoing manual reviews, automated scans, and assessments of vendor\'s systems and practices as they relate to the processing of personal information received from Pinnacle.

> **(g) Notification of Inability to Comply.** Vendor must notify Pinnacle promptly if vendor determines that it can no longer meet its obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. Upon receipt of such notification, Pinnacle shall have the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate the unauthorized use of personal information, up to and including termination of the DPA/MSA.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor agrees to cooperate with Pinnacle in responding to CCPA/CPRA consumer requests, including the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), and the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), within timelines consistent with the statute. Under the CCPA/CPRA, Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor\'s cooperation must be sufficiently prompt to allow Pinnacle to meet these deadlines.

**Fallback:** If the vendor\'s DPA template contains no CCPA/CPRA provisions whatsoever, Pinnacle will require a **standalone CCPA/CPRA Addendum** appended to the DPA. The addendum must contain all of the provisions listed in subparagraphs (a) through (g) above and must be expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should use the template language provided in Appendix B as a starting point for drafting the addendum.

Audit provisions are a cornerstone of any effective DPA. Pinnacle\'s ability to verify vendor compliance with HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR depends on having contractual audit rights that are robust enough to cover all data processing locations, including subprocessor facilities, and all relevant compliance domains. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s audit right requirements.

**Must-have:** Pinnacle must have the contractual right to audit vendor\'s data processing activities, directly or through a qualified third-party auditor designated by Pinnacle. The scope of the audit right must include:

> **(b) All subprocessor facilities** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. This requirement is critical where subprocessors operate in different jurisdictions from the vendor (e.g., a US subprocessor handling EU data under a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer). Subprocessor audit coverage is essential to verifying end-to-end compliance with the data protection requirements applicable to Pinnacle\'s data.

> **(d) Vendor\'s compliance with HIPAA Security Rule safeguards** specifically, including administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312), where vendor is a Business Associate.
**Must-have:** Audit rights must extend to subprocessor locations. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with one of the following mechanisms for subprocessor audit coverage:
> \(i\) Vendor grants Pinnacle **direct audit rights** over subprocessor facilities, with the same scope and frequency as Pinnacle\'s audit rights over vendor; or

> \(ii\) Vendor **contractually requires** each subprocessor to submit to audits by Pinnacle or Pinnacle\'s designated auditor, and provides Pinnacle with the contractual right to exercise such audits; or

> \(iii\) At minimum, vendor requires each subprocessor to **provide SOC 2 Type II reports** and/or **ISO 27001 certifications** covering the relevant data processing services, with copies provided to Pinnacle upon request no less frequently than annually.

**Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle prefers the right to conduct **two (2) audits per calendar year**: one planned audit and one for-cause audit. Planned audits should require **fifteen (15) days\' prior written notice** to the vendor. For-cause audits, triggered by a breach, suspected breach, or other compliance concern, should require **no advance notice** to the vendor.
**Fallback:** One (1) planned audit per calendar year with **thirty (30) days\' prior written notice** is acceptable, provided that the following conditions are met:
> \(a\) For-cause audits are permitted **without notice** following a confirmed or suspected breach, a regulatory inquiry, or a material compliance concern identified by Pinnacle;
> \(b\) Audit scope extends to **all data processing locations**, including subprocessor sites, as described above;

> \(c\) Vendor provides **current SOC 2 Type II reports** and **ISO 27001 certifications** as a supplement to (not a replacement for) on-site audits, with reports and certifications provided to Pinnacle within thirty (30) days of request; and

> \(d\) Vendor cooperates fully with the audit, including by providing access to relevant personnel, documentation, and systems, and by making reasonable workspace available to Pinnacle\'s audit team during on-site audits.

**Red line:** Audit rights limited to a single vendor facility (excluding subprocessor sites) are **unacceptable**. Such a limitation would prevent Pinnacle from verifying compliance at the locations where data processing actually occurs, particularly where the vendor relies on subprocessors for hosting, storage, or processing activities. If vendor refuses to extend audit scope to subprocessor facilities, the negotiator must escalate immediately to Margaret Yuen-Park.
**[8.2 HIPAA Audit Requirements]{.underline}**

Under HIPAA, Pinnacle as Covered Entity must be able to audit Business Associates for compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule and Privacy Rule. The DPA/BAA must expressly state that Pinnacle\'s audit rights include the right to evaluate vendor\'s HIPAA compliance, including without limitation:
> • Review of vendor\'s HIPAA risk assessments (required under 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A));
> • Review of vendor\'s security incident logs and breach response records;
> • Interviews with vendor\'s HIPAA Privacy Officer and HIPAA Security Officer (or equivalents); and

The HIPAA audit right must be independent of and in addition to any general audit right under the DPA. If the DPA\'s general audit provision is narrower than what HIPAA requires, the BAA must include a separate, broader audit provision that addresses the HIPAA-specific requirements listed above.
**[Section 9: Data Return, Deletion, and Retention]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the provisions governing the disposition of data at the end of the vendor relationship, including the critical interplay between post-termination data deletion obligations and HIPAA\'s six-year record retention requirement. Getting these provisions right is essential to ensuring both a clean transition and ongoing regulatory compliance.
**[9.2 HIPAA Record Retention]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must acknowledge and account for HIPAA\'s **six (6) year record retention requirement** under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later. The categories of documentation subject to this requirement include:
> • The BAA itself;
> • Security incident and breach response records;
> • Access logs and audit trails related to PHI; and
> • Any other documentation required to demonstrate compliance with HIPAA requirements.

**Must-have:** The six-year HIPAA retention obligation must be **expressly reconciled** with the post-termination deletion obligation set forth in Section 9.1 above. Without an express reconciliation, the deletion obligation and the retention obligation create an internal contradiction that could result in either premature deletion of HIPAA-required records or indefinite retention of PHI without adequate contractual protections. Pinnacle\'s recommended reconciliation language is as follows:

> *\"Notwithstanding the deletion obligations in this Section, Processor shall retain such records as are required to comply with HIPAA record retention requirements (45 CFR § 164.530(j)) for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when such records were last in effect, whichever is later. Such retained records shall remain subject to the confidentiality, security, and use restrictions of this Agreement and the Business Associate Agreement for the duration of the retention period. Upon expiration of the applicable retention period, Processor shall securely delete all such retained records and provide Controller with written certification of deletion.\"*

**Red line:** Any post-termination deletion clause that does not carve out HIPAA record retention requirements is **non-compliant** and creates significant regulatory risk. A vendor that deletes HIPAA-required documentation within 30 or 60 days of termination may be in violation of 45 CFR § 164.530(j), and Pinnacle could face enforcement consequences if it cannot produce required documentation during an OCR investigation. Negotiators must ensure that the HIPAA retention carve-out is included in every DPA involving PHI. If a vendor\'s DPA template contains a blanket deletion-at-termination clause without a HIPAA carve-out, the clause must be redlined before execution. Escalate immediately if the vendor refuses to include the carve-out.
**[Section 10: Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

Governing law and dispute resolution provisions are critical in DPAs that cover both US and EU data, particularly where the vendor is a non-US entity. A DPA that applies a single non-US governing law and non-US dispute resolution forum to all disputes --- including disputes involving US PHI and California personal information --- could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to enforce its US regulatory rights and may be inconsistent with the jurisdictional framework of HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA enforcement. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required approach: a bifurcated governing law and dispute resolution structure.
**[10.1 Bifurcated Governing Law]{.underline}**

> **(a) US Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **US data** --- including PHI, ePHI, CCPA/CPRA-covered personal information, and any other personal data of US-based data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **State of Delaware**, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Delaware law is Pinnacle\'s preferred governing law for US data disputes because Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation, Delaware has a well-developed body of commercial law, and the Delaware courts have extensive experience with complex commercial and data-related disputes.

> **(b) EU/EEA Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **EU/EEA data** --- including GDPR-covered personal data of EU/EEA data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **applicable EU/EEA Member State**. Where Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. is the contracting controller, the law of the **Netherlands** is preferred. Where the vendor is based in Germany and strongly resists Dutch law, **German law** is an acceptable alternative for EU data disputes.

**Fallback:** German law for EU data disputes is acceptable, provided that Delaware law for US data disputes is preserved as a must-have. The bifurcation itself --- applying US law to US data disputes and EU law to EU data disputes --- is the critical structural requirement. Pinnacle will not accept a DPA that applies a single non-US governing law (e.g., German law) to disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information.
**[10.2 Dispute Resolution Forum]{.underline}**

> **(a) US Data Disputes.** The parties consent to the exclusive jurisdiction of the **United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, Austin Division**, or, where federal subject matter jurisdiction is unavailable, the **state courts of Travis County, Texas**, for all disputes arising from or related to the processing of US data. This forum selection reflects the location of Pinnacle\'s principal offices and the location of Pinnacle\'s primary US data processing operations.

> **(b) EU Data Disputes.** For disputes arising from or related to the processing of EU/EEA data, arbitration under recognized EU arbitration rules is acceptable. Pinnacle will accept arbitration administered by:

**Fallback:** Pinnacle will accept arbitration for EU data disputes but will **NOT** accept non-US arbitration or non-US courts for disputes involving US data (PHI, CCPA-covered data, or any other US personal information). Any vendor DPA that applies a non-US governing law and/or a non-US dispute resolution forum to US data disputes must be **redlined**. Escalate to Margaret Yuen-Park and Rachel Osterfeld (Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP) if the vendor insists on a non-US forum for US data disputes.

> • HIPAA enforcement is under **US federal jurisdiction**. An arbitration clause seated in Munich may not be enforceable against an OCR subpoena or investigation, and may create practical barriers to Pinnacle\'s enforcement of its HIPAA-related contractual rights.

> • CCPA/CPRA enforcement is under **California jurisdiction** (California Attorney General and the California Privacy Protection Agency). A German arbitration clause may create uncertainty regarding the enforceability of CCPA-related contractual provisions.

While this playbook focuses primarily on US requirements, cross-border data transfers directly affect US data and must be addressed in vendor DPA negotiations. For example, EU data may be transferred to the US for disaster recovery or support purposes, and US data may be accessed remotely by vendor personnel located in the EU or other jurisdictions. The DPA must establish clear transfer mechanisms and documentation requirements for all such scenarios.

**Must-have:** Where vendor or any subprocessor transfers personal data from the EU/EEA to a third country (including the United States), the DPA must specify the applicable lawful transfer mechanism for each transfer scenario. Acceptable transfer mechanisms include:

> **(a) EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021. The appropriate module must be selected for each transfer relationship:
> • **Module 2** (Controller-to-Processor): For transfers from Pinnacle EU B.V. (as Controller) to a vendor (as Processor) located outside the EEA;
> • **Module 3** (Processor-to-Subprocessor): For transfers from a vendor (as Processor) to a subprocessor located outside the EEA; and
> • **Module 4** (Processor-to-Controller): Where applicable, for reverse transfers.

> **(b) EU-US Data Privacy Framework (\"DPF\")** certification: Acceptable only if the receiving entity (vendor or subprocessor) is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities. Negotiators should verify the vendor\'s DPF certification status on the International Trade Administration\'s Data Privacy Framework List (dataprivacyframework.gov) before relying on this mechanism.
**Must-have:** The DPA must address **all** transfer scenarios, including:
> • Primary data hosting and processing transfers (e.g., data stored in an EEA data center and processed by a US-based vendor);
> • Disaster recovery and business continuity transfers (e.g., data replicated to a US-based backup facility);
> • Subprocessor transfers (e.g., vendor engages a subprocessor in a third country to perform specific processing activities).

**Must-have:** Vendor must conduct and document a **Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\")** for each transfer of personal data to a third country. The TIA must assess the laws and practices of the recipient country that may affect the protection of the transferred data, including government surveillance laws, and must be made available to Pinnacle upon request. Where the TIA identifies risks that cannot be mitigated by supplementary measures, the transfer mechanism may need to be reconsidered.

**Must-have:** If a subprocessor is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, SCCs must be executed with the appropriate module (typically Module 3, Processor-to-Subprocessor) before any personal data is transferred to that subprocessor.

**Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle pre-approves the specific SCC modules for each transfer relationship during DPA negotiation, ensuring clarity and reducing the need for post-execution amendments as transfer relationships evolve.

**Fallback:** If vendor\'s DPA template attaches only one SCC module (which is common), Pinnacle will require the addition of all applicable modules before execution. The negotiator should assess the vendor\'s transfer relationships and subprocessor arrangements to determine which modules are required and ensure that they are included in the DPA as executed.

Vendors frequently engage subprocessors to perform specific data processing activities on their behalf. Because Pinnacle\'s data may ultimately be processed by entities with which Pinnacle has no direct contractual relationship, the DPA must include robust subprocessor requirements that ensure end-to-end protection. This Section works in conjunction with Section 8 (Audit Rights --- subprocessor coverage) and Section 4 (HIPAA BAA --- subcontractor flow-down).

**Must-have:** Vendor must impose on each subprocessor **substantially the same** data protection obligations as those imposed on vendor under the DPA. This flow-down requirement applies to all applicable regulatory regimes, including:

> • **HIPAA BAA flow-down terms**: Each subprocessor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI must be bound by BAA obligations equivalent to those in vendor\'s BAA with Pinnacle (per 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));

> • **CCPA/CPRA Service Provider restrictions**: Each subprocessor that processes California personal information must be contractually restricted from selling, sharing, combining, or using the personal information for purposes other than those specified in the agreement;

> • **GDPR Article 28 requirements**: Each subprocessor must be bound by a written contract that provides the same level of data protection as the vendor\'s DPA with Pinnacle (per GDPR Art. 28(4)); and
> • **Confidentiality obligations**: Each subprocessor must be bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as those in the DPA.

**Must-have:** Vendor remains **fully liable** for the acts and omissions of its subprocessors. The DPA must include an express statement that vendor shall be responsible for the performance of its subprocessors as if such acts or omissions were vendor\'s own. The use of subprocessors does not relieve vendor of any of its obligations under the DPA.
**Must-have:** The DPA must include a **current list of all authorized subprocessors**, specifying for each subprocessor:
> • Description of the data processing activities performed by the subprocessor.
This list must be appended to the DPA as an exhibit or schedule and must be updated whenever a subprocessor is added, removed, or changed.

**Must-have:** Pinnacle (as Controller) must be notified of any proposed new subprocessor or change to existing subprocessors with **sufficient time to assess and object** to the change before it becomes effective. The DPA must provide Pinnacle with a meaningful objection right --- that is, the right to object to a proposed subprocessor and, if the objection is not resolved, the right to terminate the DPA without penalty.

**Nice-to-have:** A **thirty (30) day objection window** for new subprocessors, measured from the date of vendor\'s notification to Pinnacle. This provides Pinnacle with adequate time to assess the proposed subprocessor\'s data protection capabilities, conduct due diligence, and raise any concerns before the subprocessor begins processing Pinnacle\'s data.

**Fallback:** An objection window of **fourteen (14) to fifteen (15) calendar days** is acceptable and is consistent with current market norms for DPA negotiations. However, the objection window must not be shorter than fourteen (14) days, and the notification must include sufficient detail about the proposed subprocessor (including the information listed above) to enable Pinnacle to make an informed assessment.
> **(b) HIPAA Security Rule categories** --- Where vendor is a Business Associate, the DPA/BAA must require implementation of:
> • **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity mechanisms, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.

> Both the GDPR and HIPAA security frameworks must be explicitly referenced in the DPA. A DPA that references only GDPR Article 32 without addressing the HIPAA Security Rule is insufficient for vendors that process PHI.

Pinnacle has obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR to respond to requests from individuals (patients, consumers, and data subjects) exercising their data protection rights. Because vendors often hold or process the data necessary to respond to these requests, vendor cooperation is essential. This Section sets forth the requirements for vendor assistance with data subject and consumer rights requests.

> **HIPAA --- Individual Access Rights.** Under 45 CFR § 164.524, individuals have the right to access their PHI. Pinnacle must provide access within **thirty (30) days** of the request, with one **thirty (30) day extension** permitted upon written notice to the individual. Vendor must cooperate with Pinnacle to identify, locate, and produce the requested PHI within a timeframe that enables Pinnacle to meet this regulatory deadline.

> **CCPA/CPRA --- Consumer Rights.** Under the CCPA/CPRA, California consumers have the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), and the right to limit use of sensitive personal information (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.121). Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in fulfilling these requests, including by searching vendor\'s systems for the consumer\'s personal information, executing deletion or correction instructions, and confirming completion.
> • **HIPAA BAA obligations**, for as long as vendor retains any PHI, and in any event for the six (6) year record retention period under 45 CFR § 164.530(j).

**Note on HIPAA Survival:** HIPAA requires six (6) years of record retention under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Any DPA survival period shorter than six (6) years may be insufficient for HIPAA purposes, because the termination of the DPA\'s protective provisions before the end of the retention period would leave PHI-related documentation without contractual protections. Where a vendor proposes a shorter survival period (e.g., two (2) years), Pinnacle must negotiate either:

> \(b\) A carve-out providing that HIPAA-related obligations (including the BAA, security obligations, audit rights, and confidentiality obligations as they relate to PHI) survive for the full **six (6) year retention period** or for as long as vendor retains any PHI, whichever is longer, even if the general DPA survival period is shorter.

**Fallback:** A general DPA survival period of **two (2) to three (3) years** is acceptable for non-HIPAA obligations, provided that HIPAA obligations have a separate, longer survival as described above. The negotiator should ensure that the survival clause clearly distinguishes between the general survival period and the HIPAA-specific survival period, and that the HIPAA survival is not inadvertently overridden by the general survival provision.
**Standard DPAs**       Annual fees under \$1,000,000; no PHI; no cross-border transfers                                                          Senior Privacy Counsel
**Complex DPAs**        Annual fees \$1,000,000--\$5,000,000; or involves PHI; or involves cross-border transfers                                 Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel
> \(a\) **Vendor refuses to execute a BAA** where vendor processes PHI;
> \(b\) **Vendor proposes a liability cap below 2x annual fees** for data protection claims;
> \(c\) **Vendor refuses audit rights** over subprocessor facilities;
> \(d\) **Vendor applies non-US governing law** to US data disputes (i.e., disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information);
> \(f\) **Vendor refuses CCPA/CPRA Service Provider certification language** required under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d).

**(1) HIPAA BAA Integration**              Fully compliant BAA, integrated or incorporated by reference; all mandatory provisions per 45 CFR § 164.504(e)                                                                                 BAA integrated into DPA body rather than separate exhibit                                   Standalone BAA exhibit, expressly incorporated, executed simultaneously with DPA                        Vendor refuses to execute a BAA for PHI processing --- escalate immediately

**(2) Breach Notification Timeline**       Vendor notifies Pinnacle within 24 hours of discovery of actual or suspected breach                                                                                                            Preliminary telephonic notice within 4 hours; written notice within 24 hours                24 hours is firm; no fallback beyond 24 hours                                                           Vendor proposes timeline exceeding 24 hours --- reject and redline

**(4) Consequential Damages**              No blanket exclusion for data breaches involving willful misconduct; uncapped liability for willful misconduct, gross negligence, intentional confidentiality breaches, and regulatory fines   Uncapped liability for all data protection claims                                           Exclusion acceptable for general claims but NOT for willful misconduct data breaches                    Blanket consequential damages exclusion for all data protection claims --- reject

**(5) CCPA/CPRA Service Provider Terms**   All seven Service Provider provisions (Sec. 7.1(a)-(g)) including certification language                                                                                                       Cooperation with consumer rights requests within 5 business days                            Standalone CCPA/CPRA Addendum if DPA template lacks CCPA provisions                                     Vendor refuses Service Provider certification --- escalate to GC

**(6) Audit Rights --- Scope**             Covers all vendor and subprocessor data processing locations; includes HIPAA Security Rule assessment                                                                                          Two audits/year (one planned, one for-cause); 15 days\' notice for planned                  One planned audit/year with 30 days\' notice; for-cause without notice; SOC 2/ISO 27001 as supplement   Audit limited to single vendor facility (excludes subprocessors) --- escalate

**(7) Data Return/Deletion**               Data return option in machine-readable format; 30-day transition assistance; deletion within 30 days of return completion (60 days max)                                                        Data return in Pinnacle\'s preferred format with metadata intact                            90-day deletion window acceptable if return option and transition assistance preserved                  Vendor refuses any data return option (deletion-only) --- escalate

**(8) HIPAA Record Retention**             6-year retention per 45 CFR § 164.530(j); express carve-out from deletion obligation; retained records subject to ongoing DPA protections                                                      N/A --- regulatory requirement, not negotiable                                              N/A --- regulatory requirement, not negotiable                                                          Post-termination deletion clause without HIPAA retention carve-out --- escalate

**(9) Governing Law**                      Bifurcated: Delaware law for US data disputes; Netherlands (preferred) or applicable EU law for EU data disputes                                                                               Delaware law for all matters                                                                German law acceptable for EU disputes; Delaware law for US disputes is firm                             Non-US law applied to US data disputes --- escalate

**(10) Dispute Resolution**                US: Western District of Texas (Austin) or Travis County courts; EU: DIS, ICC, or LCIA arbitration                                                                                              Federal court for all disputes                                                              Arbitration for EU matters acceptable; US courts for US matters is firm                                 Non-US forum for US data disputes --- escalate

**(11) International Transfers**           SCCs with correct module for each transfer scenario; DPF where certified; TIA for each third-country transfer                                                                                  Pre-approval of specific SCC modules during negotiation                                     Require addition of missing SCC modules before execution                                                DPA fails to address applicable transfer scenarios --- redline

**(12) Subprocessor Flow-Down**            Substantially same obligations; vendor fully liable; current subprocessor list; notification and objection right                                                                               30-day objection window                                                                     14--15 day objection window                                                                             No subprocessor flow-down or no notification/objection right --- reject
**[B.1 BAA Integration Clause]{.underline}**

*\"This Data Processing Agreement incorporates the Business Associate Agreement attached hereto as Exhibit \[\_\] (the \'BAA\'), which is hereby made an integral part of this Agreement. In the event of any conflict between the terms of this Agreement and the terms of the BAA with respect to the processing, use, or disclosure of Protected Health Information (as defined in 45 CFR § 160.103), the more protective provision shall govern. The BAA shall remain in effect for the duration of this Agreement and, to the extent Processor retains any Protected Health Information following termination, for so long as Processor maintains such Protected Health Information.\"*

*\"Processor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under or in connection with this Data Processing Agreement shall not exceed an amount equal to two times (2x) the total fees paid or payable by Controller to Processor during the twelve (12) month period immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the liability cap set forth in this Section shall not apply to claims arising from: (a) Processor\'s willful misconduct or gross negligence; (b) Processor\'s intentional or reckless breach of confidentiality obligations; or (c) regulatory fines, penalties, or enforcement costs imposed on Controller as a direct result of Processor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws.\"*
**[B.4 CCPA/CPRA Service Provider Certification Clause]{.underline}**

*\"Controller shall have the right, at its own expense and upon reasonable prior written notice (not less than fifteen (15) days for planned audits, and without notice for for-cause audits following a confirmed or suspected Incident), to audit Processor\'s and each Subprocessor\'s compliance with this Agreement, including by inspecting data processing facilities, reviewing policies and procedures, and examining relevant records. Processor shall contractually require each Subprocessor to submit to audits by Controller or Controller\'s designated auditor on terms no less favorable than those set forth in this Section.\"*
**[B.7 Bifurcated Governing Law Clause]{.underline}**

*Cloud Infrastructure · Managed Databases · Analytics*
This Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") forms part of and is subject to the terms of the Master Services Agreement (\"Agreement\" or \"MSA\") between the Processor and the Controller.

This DPA is designed to ensure compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 (the \"GDPR\") and applicable data protection laws governing the Processing of Personal Data in connection with the Services provided under the Agreement.
**Processor Registered Office:**
Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Hohenzollernstraße 88 80796 Munich, Germany
Handelsregister HRB 247891, Amtsgericht München (Munich Local Court)
**Prepared by:**
Legal Department, Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH
**Contact:**
Dr. Florian Neumann Chief Legal Officer Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH
Email: florian.neumann@stratospherecloud.example.com
Right-click to update Table of Contents
**[RECITALS]{.underline}**

**WHEREAS**, the Controller and the Processor have entered into a Master Services Agreement dated \\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\*\\* (the \"Agreement\") pursuant to which the Processor provides cloud hosting, managed database services, and analytics support to the Controller in connection with the Controller\'s business operations;

**WHEREAS**, in the course of providing the Services under the Agreement, the Processor will Process Personal Data on behalf of the Controller, and such Processing may involve the collection, storage, retrieval, use, disclosure by transmission, combination, restriction, erasure, and destruction of Personal Data as further described in Annex A to this DPA;

**WHEREAS**, the Parties wish to ensure that such Processing of Personal Data complies with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (the \"General Data Protection Regulation\" or \"GDPR\"), as well as applicable data protection laws of the European Union and its Member States;

**WHEREAS**, the Parties intend for this DPA to set forth their respective obligations with respect to the Processing of Personal Data in connection with the Agreement, including without limitation the Processor\'s obligations as a data processor within the meaning of Article 4(8) and Article 28 of the GDPR; and

**WHEREAS**, the Parties agree that this DPA, together with the Annexes attached hereto, constitutes the binding agreement between them with respect to the Processing of Personal Data under the Agreement and shall supplement and form an integral part of the Agreement;

**NOW, THEREFORE**, in consideration of the mutual obligations set forth herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the Parties agree as follows:
**[SECTION 1 --- DEFINITIONS]{.underline}**

**1.1** \"**Applicable Data Protection Law**\" means Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (the GDPR) and any applicable legislation of the European Union or its Member States implementing, supplementing, or replacing the GDPR, including without limitation the German Federal Data Protection Act (*Bundesdatenschutzgesetz*, \"BDSG\") as amended from time to time, and any other data protection legislation directly applicable within the European Economic Area.

**1.2** \"**Controller**\" means the natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the Processing of Personal Data, as defined in Article 4(7) of the GDPR, and as identified in the signature block of this DPA.

**1.3** \"**Data Subject**\" means an identified or identifiable natural person to whom Personal Data relates, as defined in Article 4(1) of the GDPR. 195: **[Section 4: HIPAA Business Associate Agreement Requirements]{.underline}**
196: 
197: This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Failure to execute a compliant BAA with a vendor that processes PHI exposes Pinnacle to enforcement action by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (\"**OCR**\"), including civil monetary penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year (as adjusted for inflation). Equally important, the absence of a BAA means that any disclosure of PHI to the vendor may itself constitute a HIPAA violation.
198: 
199: ALL vendors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on Pinnacle\'s behalf must execute a BAA. There are no exceptions to this requirement. This Section sets forth the must-have, nice-to-have, and fallback positions for BAA terms, as well as non-negotiable red lines.
200: 
201: **[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**
202: 
203: **Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.
204: 
205: The BAA must specify, at a minimum, the following terms:
206: 
207: > **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. The BAA should enumerate the specific permitted purposes and should include a catch-all restriction providing that any use or disclosure not expressly authorized is prohibited.
208: >
209: > **(b) Minimum Necessary Standard.** The BAA must require vendor compliance with the \"minimum necessary\" standard set forth in 45 CFR § 164.502(b). Vendor must limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of each use, disclosure, or request. Vendor must implement policies and procedures to identify the workforce members who need access to PHI and to limit each such workforce member\'s access to the minimum PHI necessary for that person\'s role.
210: >
211: > **(c) Workforce Training.** Vendor must train all workforce members who have access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements. Training must be provided upon hiring and at least annually thereafter. Vendor must maintain documentation of training completion and make such documentation available to Pinnacle upon reasonable request.
212: >
213: > **(d) HIPAA Security Rule Safeguards.** Vendor must implement and maintain safeguards consistent with the three categories of the HIPAA Security Rule:
214: >
215: > \(i\) **Administrative safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.308, including risk analysis and risk management, security management processes, workforce security, information access management, security awareness and training, security incident procedures, contingency planning, and evaluation;
216: >
217: > \(ii\) **Physical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.310, including facility access controls, workstation use and security, and device and media controls; and
218: >
219: > \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.
220: >
221: > **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). This flow-down obligation must be contractually documented between vendor and each such subcontractor before PHI is made available to the subcontractor.
222: >
223: > **(f) Breach Notification.** The BAA must include breach notification obligations consistent with the HITECH Act requirements, as described in detail in Section 5 of this playbook.
224: >
225: > **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). This includes the BAA itself, policies and procedures relating to the protection of PHI, workforce training records, incident response records, and risk assessment documentation.
226: >
227: > **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.
228: 
229: **Nice-to-have:** The BAA should be integrated directly into the DPA body rather than attached as a separate exhibit. Integration reduces the risk of gaps in coverage that can arise when the DPA and BAA are separate documents with potentially inconsistent terms, different effective dates, or different amendment procedures. An integrated BAA also simplifies contract management and ensures that the BAA\'s security and audit provisions are consistent with the corresponding DPA provisions.
230: 
231: **Fallback:** A standalone BAA exhibit is acceptable if the following conditions are met: (i) the BAA exhibit is expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference; (ii) the BAA cross-references the DPA\'s security, audit, and breach notification provisions to ensure consistency; (iii) the BAA is executed simultaneously with the DPA and by the same authorized signatories; and (iv) the BAA includes a provision stating that, in the event of a conflict between the BAA and the DPA, the more protective provision governs with respect to the handling of PHI.
232: 
233: **[4.2 BAA Negotiation Red Lines]{.underline}**
234: 
235: Pinnacle will **NOT** execute a DPA without a conforming BAA where the vendor processes PHI. This is a **non-negotiable requirement** driven by federal law. No business justification, no vendor relationship importance, and no time pressure overrides this requirement.
236: 
237: If a vendor refuses to execute a BAA, or if a vendor\'s proposed BAA is materially deficient and the vendor refuses to negotiate acceptable terms, the negotiator must **escalate immediately** to Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel, and to Rachel Osterfeld at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP. Under no circumstances should a negotiator proceed with DPA execution in the absence of a conforming BAA.
238: 
239: For context, Pinnacle currently has approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts** whose PHI may be processed by vendors in the course of providing services to Pinnacle. The regulatory and reputational exposure associated with unauthorized disclosure of this PHI is substantial. OCR enforcement actions in recent years have resulted in settlements and penalties ranging from \$100,000 to over \$16 million for HIPAA violations involving inadequate BAA protections.
240: 
241: Negotiators should also be aware that some vendors may propose a \"HIPAA addendum\" or \"healthcare data supplement\" that purports to address HIPAA requirements but does not contain all of the mandatory BAA provisions listed in Section 4.1 above. Such documents must be carefully reviewed against the checklist in Section 4.1, and any missing provisions must be added before execution.
242: 
243: **[Section 5: Breach Notification]{.underline}**
244: 
245: Breach notification provisions are among the most operationally significant terms in any DPA. The speed and completeness of vendor breach notification directly affects Pinnacle\'s ability to assess the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and meet its own notification obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s breach notification requirements, which are in certain respects **more restrictive** than the standalone requirements of any single applicable regulation.
246: 
247: Pinnacle\'s internal data breach response standard, as adopted by the Board of Directors in October 2023, requires that the Company\'s Incident Response Team be activated within **four (4) hours** of receiving vendor notification of a breach or suspected breach. This internal standard drives the 24-hour vendor notification requirement described below; a vendor notification timeline of 48 hours or longer is insufficient to support Pinnacle\'s internal response protocols and downstream regulatory obligations.
248: 
249: **[5.1 Notification Timeline]{.underline}**
250: 
251: **Must-have:** Vendor must notify Pinnacle of any actual or reasonably suspected breach of Personal Data, PHI, or California Personal Information within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. For purposes of this requirement, \"**discovery**\" means the first day on which the breach is known to the vendor, or the first day on which the breach, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to the vendor. This definition is consistent with the HITECH Act\'s definition of discovery at 42 U.S.C. § 17382.
252: 
253: The 24-hour notification obligation applies regardless of whether the breach is confirmed or still under investigation. Pinnacle recognizes that a vendor\'s initial notification may be preliminary and that additional information will become available as the investigation proceeds. However, the failure to provide timely preliminary notification --- even where the full scope of the breach is not yet known --- deprives Pinnacle of the ability to initiate its own assessment and response activities.
254: 
255: Notification must be directed to Pinnacle\'s Chief Privacy Officer, Dr. Anand Krishnamurthy, at privacy-incidents@pinnaclehealth.com and by telephone at (512) 555-0199 (available 24/7), with a copy to the General Counsel\'s office at legal-notices@pinnaclehealth.com.
256: 
257: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides **preliminary telephonic notification** within **four (4) hours** of discovery, followed by **written notification** within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. The telephonic notification should include the vendor\'s initial assessment of the nature of the incident, the categories of data potentially affected, and the vendor\'s immediate containment measures. This telephonic-plus-written approach allows Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team to begin its assessment in parallel with the vendor\'s investigation.
258: 
259: **Fallback:** The 24-hour notification timeline is a **firm requirement**. Pinnacle will not accept timelines exceeding 24 hours for processor-to-controller notification. Negotiators should be aware that many vendor DPA templates propose **48-hour** or **72-hour** notification timelines. These proposals must be rejected and redlined to 24 hours. The following talking points may be useful in negotiations:
260: 
261: > • The **72-hour timeline** referenced in GDPR Article 33(1) is the *controller\'s* obligation to notify the *supervisory authority*, not the processor\'s obligation to notify the controller. GDPR Article 33(2) requires processors to notify controllers \"without undue delay after becoming aware\" of a breach, which the European Data Protection Board has interpreted as requiring notification significantly faster than 72 hours.
262: >
263: > • A **48-hour** processor-to-controller timeline is insufficient because it compresses Pinnacle\'s time to assess the breach, engage legal counsel, activate its incident response plan, and prepare its own regulatory notifications. Under HIPAA, Pinnacle must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, and discovery is deemed to occur when the Business Associate notifies the Covered Entity. Under CCPA/CPRA, California\'s data breach notification statute (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.82) requires notification \"in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.\" Every hour of delay in vendor notification reduces Pinnacle\'s available response window.
